books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, A. Migrations and New Communities in the Age of the Market Revolution
Irish Immigration in the Early 19th century

stimulus.text:
Immigration to the United States, by decade (alien passengers arriving; Statistical Abstract of the United States):

| Decade | Immigrants |
| --- | ---: |
| 1821–1830 | 143,439 |
| 1831–1840 | 599,125 |
| 1841–1850 | 1,713,251 |

Figures are totals for each ten-year period.
stimulus.source_note: Statistical Abstract of the United States, Table 107, Immigration 1821 to 1943 (U.S. Census Bureau). Figures verified against the Census Bureau publication.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The sharp rise in the 1840s shown in the table is best explained by

options.text: the end of the War of 1812
options.misconception: The war ended in 1815, thirty years before the 1840s surge.

options.text: the discovery of gold in California
options.misconception: Gold was found in 1848, at the very end of the decade, and it drew Americans west more than immigrants across the Atlantic.

options.text: the opening of the Erie Canal
options.misconception: The canal opened in 1825 and moved goods inside America; it did not bring immigrants across the ocean.

rationales.A: The war ended in 1815. A surge thirty years later needs a cause from the 1840s, not from 1815.
rationales.B: Gold was found in 1848, too late to explain a decade-long surge, and it pulled Americans west rather than bringing Europeans over.
rationales.C: The 1840s jump lines up with the Irish potato famine of 1845-1852. About a million Irish starved and another million came to the United States, most settling in Northeast port cities.
rationales.D: The Erie Canal moved freight between Buffalo and New York. It carried no one across the Atlantic.
rationales.general:
1. Date the surge. The big jump is the 1840s, from about 599,000 to about 1,713,000.
2. Date each choice. The war ended in 1815, the canal opened in 1825, gold came in 1848.
3. Keep the cause in the same decade. The potato famine struck in 1845.
Background: Blight ruined the potato, the staple food of the Irish poor.
Remember: a cause must sit in the same time as its effect, so date every choice.
